abstract: Dr. Calvert provides an interactive lecture on female vulvar examination and common pathologies encountered in family medicine. The talk covers benign conditions such as urethral caruncle, Bartholin cyst, and Gartner duct cyst, as well as premalignant and malignant lesions including vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) and vulvar cancer. Emphasis is placed on the importance of thorough physical examination, palpation to detect subtle changes in texture, and a low threshold for biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain. Clinical pearls include recognizing painless syphilitic chancres, distinguishing infected from noninfected Bartholin cysts, and avoiding reliance on emergency department evaluations for vaginal complaints without performing a pelvic exam.
key_points: Urethral caruncle is a common benign lesion in older women that presents with blood on the tissue; typically no treatment is needed, but symptomatic lesions can be removed by suture ligation of the stalk.
Bartholin cysts: infected cysts present with severe pain and require incision and drainage with a word catheter; noninfected cysts with clear fluid may be associated with cancer and warrant biopsy.
Vaginal dysplasia (VIN) can be very subtle, appearing as a pale or red color change with palpable thickness; always palpate and biopsy any suspicious area.
Lichen sclerosus lacks distinct margination, which helps differentiate it from VIN.
Syphilis chancres are characteristically painless, asking about pain can help distinguish from other ulcerative lesions.
Gartner duct cysts are often identified in newborns by family physicians; they usually require no intervention unless complicated by infection or obstructing delivery.
Urethral diverticulum is confirmed by MRI; it presents as a cystic structure near the urethra and may require surgical management.
Always perform a pelvic exam for vaginal complaints; relying on emergency department assessments may lead to missed diagnoses, as illustrated by a case of advanced VIN.
When uncertain about a vulvar lesion, perform a punch or shave biopsy, it is minor surgery and provides definitive diagnosis.
Palpation of lesions is critical: warts feel soft and mushy, while dysplastic or malignant areas feel thick, firm, or have depth.
